'''''Phormium tenax''''' (called '''flax''' in [[New Zealand English]]; {{lang|mi|harakeke}} in [[Māori language|Māori]]; '''New Zealand flax'''<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 18 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="Chitham 2019 111">{{Cite book |last=Chitham |first=Karl |title=Crafting Aotearoa : a cultural history of making in New Zealand and the wider Moana Oceania |publisher=Te Papa Press |others=Kolokesa Uafā Māhina-Tuai, Damian Skinner, Rigel Sorzano |year=2019 |isbn=978-0-9941362-7-5 |location=Wellington, New Zealand |pages=111 |oclc=1118996645}}</ref> outside New Zealand; and '''New Zealand hemp'''<ref name=GRIN/> in historical nautical contexts) is an evergreen [[perennial]] plant native to [[New Zealand]] and [[Norfolk Island]] that is an important [[fiber|fibre]] plant and a popular ornamental plant.<ref name="HolmesEtAl">Roger Holmes and Lance Walheim. 2005. ''California Home Landscaping'', Creative Homeowner Press {{ISBN|978-1-58011-254-3}}</ref>  The plant grows as a clump of long, straplike leaves, up to two metres long, from which arises a much taller flowering shoot, with dramatic yellow or red flowers.<ref name="HolmesEtAl" />

Despite being commonly known as 'flax', harakeke is of the genus ''Phormium'', a monocot, and is a leaf fibre, whereas flax (linen) is of the genus ''Linum'', a rosid, and is a bast fibre (which comes from the stem of the plant). The two plants have an extremely distant evolutionary relationship with each other.

The fibre has been widely used since the arrival of [[Māori people|Māori]] to New Zealand, originally in [[Māori traditional textiles]] and also in rope and sail making<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-Gov09_02Rail-t1-body-d7-d2.html|title=Our Flax for the Navy | NZETC}}</ref><ref name="Chitham 2019 111"/> after the arrival of Europeans until at least WWII. It is an invasive species in some of the Pacific Islands and in Australia.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hear.org/pier/species/phormium_tenax.htm|title=Phormium tenax (PIER species info)|date=9 January 2011|publisher=Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER)|access-date=20 August 2012}}</ref>

The blades of the plant contain [[cucurbitacin]]s, which are poisonous to some animals, and some of them are among the bitterest tastes to humans.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)94223-7 | volume=17 | issue=4 | title=New cucurbitacins from Phormium tenax and Marah oreganus | journal=Phytochemistry | pages=767–769| year=1978 | last1=Kupchan | first1=S.Morris | last2=Meshulam | first2=Haim | last3=Sneden | first3=Albert T. | bibcode=1978PChem..17..767K }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Phormium tenax'' J.R.Forst & G.Forst was described in 1776 by [[Johann Reinhold Forster]] and [[Georg Forster]], who were the father and son team of German botanists on the [[second voyage of James Cook]].<ref>{{Cite Q|Q67939286}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The ''hara'' in the Māori name ''harakeke'' is a remnant of the [[Proto-Austronesian language|Austronesian]] root ''*paŋudaN'' (via [[Proto-Oceanic language|Proto-Oceanic]] ''*padran'') surviving in [[Austronesian languages|related languages]] referring to [[pandanus]] plants with similar characteristics of sheathing leaves also used for weaving (like ''[[Pandanus tectorius]]'', also known as ''hala'' in [[Hawaiian language|Hawaiian]]), as New Zealand was one of the only places where pandanus was not available.<ref name="temarareo">{{cite web|title=Proto-Polynesian Etymologies: *Fara|url=http://www.temarareo.org/PPN-Fara.html|access-date=15 January 2019|work=Te Mära Reo: The Language Garden|publisher=Benton Family Trust}}</ref>

==Ecology==
The [[jumping spider]] ''[[Trite planiceps]]'' lives predominantly in the rolled-up leaves of this species. ''Phormium tenax'' is a coastal cover plant associated with significant habitat such as the breeding habitat for the [[endangered]] [[yellow-eyed penguin]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=C. Michael|first=Hogan|date=April 6, 2009|title=Yellow-eyed Penguin (EN)-''Megadyptes antipodes''(Hombron & Jacquinot, 1841)|url=http://www.igoterra.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=222|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150802014621/http://www.igoterra.com/artspec_information.asp?thingid=222|archive-date=2 August 2015|website=IgoTerra}}</ref>

==Māori traditional uses==
{{Further|Flax in New Zealand}}
New Zealand flax was one of the most commonly used fibres for weaving prior to European contact in New Zealand, due to its wide availability and long strands.<ref name="Mckendry-raranga">{{Cite Q|Q106827316}}</ref> Harakeke can be woven raw to create open-weave items (where the ''para'' or the waterproof [[Epidermis (botany)|epidermis]] of the plant is kept intact), or processed so only the [[Muka (fibre)|muka]] remains, for close-weave objects.<ref name="Mckendry-raranga"/> The width and length of harakeke leaves allow weavers to create a variety of strip lengths, making the plant suitable for a range of objects and sizes.<ref name="Mckendry-raranga"/>

In pre-European society, Māori had specific plantations of flax, which was their most important textile. It was prepared by cutting the green leaves close to the base before the leaves were split and woven. Various preparations of the leaves allowed the material to be used both as a hardy flat thick-woven material (as in [[Kete (basket)|kete]] and mats) and also as a fibrous twine, used for creating both rope and finely woven cloaks.

Harakeke can be boiled with hot stones to bleach strips, however dying the fibre is difficult due to the water resistant ''para''.<ref name="Mckendry-raranga"/> However, harakeke can by dyed using ''paru'',<ref>{{Cite book |last=Chitham |first=Karl |title=Crafting Aotearoa : a cultural history of making in New Zealand and the wider Moana Oceania |publisher=Te Papa Press |others=Kolokesa Uafā Māhina-Tuai, Damian Skinner, Rigel Sorzano |year=2019 |isbn=978-0-9941362-7-5 |location=Wellington, New Zealand |pages=55 |oclc=1118996645}}</ref> or an iron-rich mud.<ref name="Mckendry-raranga"/> Harakeke can be made more flexible with less shrinkage using the ''hapine'' technique, where a knife or shell is run across the fibre to remove moisture without breaking the surface layers.<ref name="Mckendry-raranga"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McCallum |first1=Rua Elizabeth |last2=Carr |first2=Debra Julie |date=2012 |title=Identification and use of plant material for the manufacture of New Zealand indigenous woven objects |url=http://hdl.handle.net/10125/23555 |journal=Ethnobotany Research & Applications |language=en-US |volume=10 |pages=185–198 |doi=10.17348/era.10.0.185-198 |hdl=10125/23555 |issn=1547-3465|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Phormium tenax'' had many uses in traditional Māori society. It was the main material used for weaving, adopted after aute ([[paper mulberry]]), the traditional tree used to create fabric in [[Polynesia]], did not thrive in New Zealand's climate.<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Te Papa Press| isbn = 978-1-877385-56-8| last = Tamarapa| first = Awhina| title = Māori Cloaks| date = 2011}}</ref> Many of the traditional uses have largely fallen into disuse, though there is an upswing in the use of traditional materials in modern Māori art and craft. The two most common forms for flax in traditional craft are the use of stripped, dried leaves as broad bands, such as in the weaving of ''[[Kete (basket)|kete]]'' (flax baskets), and the scraping, pounding, and washing of the leaves to create a fibre — ''[[Muka (fibre)|muka]]'' — which is used in ''[[tāniko]]'' (weaving) of soft, durable fabric for clothing. Flax is also used as a decorative and structural element in ''[[tukutuku]]'', panelling found within Māori ''[[wharenui]]'' (meeting houses).

[[File: Flax worker feeding a flax leaf into the stripper ATLIB 306064 (cropped).png|thumb|A worker feeding a flax leaf into a stripper, circa 1910.]]
Prior to the [[Great Depression]] of the 1930s, which decimated flax as an industry, there were two serious attempts by Europeans to breed for fibre. The first was by [[Wellington]]-based [[Leonard Cockayne]] about 1908.<ref>{{Cite news|date=7 May 1908|title=Scientific Plant Bredding|volume=1|page=7|work=[[The Dominion (Wellington)|Dominion]]|issue=191|url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/DOM19080507.2.60}}</ref> The second by [[Massey University|Massey]]-based [[John Stuart Yeates]] in the late 1920s.<ref>{{Cite news|date=21 December 1929|title=Progress Made - Various Investigations|volume=108|work=[[Fairfax Media|Evening Post]]|issue=150|url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19291221.2.108}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=20 September 1930|title=Valuable Work Done|volume=110|work=[[Fairfax Media|Evening Post]]|issue=71|url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/EP19300920.2.20}}</ref> More recently research led by [[Xiaowen Yuan]] at [[Massey University]] has investigated the use of novel composite materials made from flax fibre to improve [[supercapacitor]] performance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Massey researchers awarded more than $13 million in MBIE funding |url=https://www.massey.ac.nz/about/news/massey-researchers-awarded-more-than-13-million-in-mbie-funding/ |access-date=2024-02-10 |website=www.massey.ac.nz |language=en-NZ}}</ref>

New Zealand Flax was cultivated on [[Saint Helena]] from the late 1800s to around 1966 for the production of string and rope and for export.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sainthelenaisland.info/flax.htm|title = The Flax Industry | Saint Helena Island Info: All about St Helena, in the South Atlantic Ocean}}</ref> Today the plants remain but the industry has stopped; they are considered an ecological problem.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sainthelenaisland.info/endemics.htm|title=Endemic Species | Saint Helena Island Info: All about St Helena, in the South Atlantic Ocean}}</ref>

===Ornamental===
In recent times, ''P. tenax'' and its cousin ''[[Phormium colensoi|P. colensoi]]'' have been widely cultivated as ornamental garden plants, their striking fans of pointed leaves providing a focal point in mixed plantings or at the edge of a lawn. They are easy to grow in a sunny spot, especially in coastal areas with some protection in winter, but require reliably moist soil. They are frequently found in garden centres amongst plants with a similar appearance, notably ''[[Yucca]]'' and ''[[Cordyline]]''. However, these are very different plants with different requirements. ''P. tenax'' and some cultivars can grow to a substantial size - {{convert|4|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|2|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} broad.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

*'Bronze Baby' - arching bronze leaves, {{convert|2|to|3|ft|m|adj=on}} plant.
*'Dazzler' - arching leaves that are bronze-maroon with red and pink stripes, plant reaches 3 feet in height

*'Sundowner'{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Phormium'' 'Sundowner'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/91178/Phormium-Sundowner-(v)/Details | access-date = 6 February 2021}}</ref> - {{convert|6|ft|m|adj=mid|-tall}} plant, leaves are striped with bronze, green and rose-pink
*'Variegatum'{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Phormium tenax'' 'Variegatum'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/97781/Phormium-tenax-Variegatum-(v)/Details | access-date = 6 February 2021}}</ref> 
*'Yellow Wave'{{smallcaps|agm}}<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Phormium'' 'Yellow Wave'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/94527/Phormium-Yellow-Wave-(v)/Details | access-date = 6 February 2021}}</ref>
